tasks.title: the history guard reads a comment, a here-string, a case body and an emitted hook the way the shell does
tasks.description: Close four residuals of the history guard and the shared line-continuation join. (1) join_continuations decides whether `#` starts a comment from the raw previous character; carry a word-start flag instead (an unescaped blank, newline or operator sets it; any other character or an escaped pair clears it; a removed backslash-newline leaves it) and treat `#` as a comment only while it is set. (2) A here-string's reader is recognised only as the first word of its command; find it past the same wrapper list the heredoc reader uses. (3) A `case` pattern's `)` inside a double-quoted substitution closes it early; a body holding a `case` with no `esac` before the close is unreadable (the command goes to the raw-text reading). (4) An emitter whose output is written to a redirect target that carries a quote or expansion, lies under a git hooks directory (.git/hooks/, .husky/, core.hooksPath), or is run later in the same command (sh/bash/source/./path/make) stays graded as the git it spells. Each with a deny case red first and an allow case beside it; SECURITY.md's residual list and CHANGELOG updated.

tasks.title: Review findings: the guards lex operators outside quotes, read only an emitter's phrase, and read a case body instead of giving up
tasks.description:
Phase review findings, all to be fixed. Decisions: (R1) the stage model lexes its own operators, recognising `|`, `>` and the rest only OUTSIDE quotes, so a quoted `>` in a commit message is text. (R2) the phrase pass applies only to a stage whose program is a text emitter (echo, printf), the one program whose arguments are what it prints. (R3) `_substitution_end` tracks `case`/`esac` in command position and treats a `)` inside an open case as a pattern's, so the body is READ rather than handed to the raw-text reading; `_open_case` goes. (R4) the stage model covers a clobber redirect, a group `( )`/`{ }` whose output is piped or redirected, every shell program _config knows plus eval, source of stdin, a program named by a variable, and tee's file operands; a process substitution, a glob or an expansion in a target is unresolvable; hook paths are matched case-insensitively and `.husky/` anywhere. (R5) SECURITY.md names what stays open (a file written by another program such as dd or cp, a phrase assembled at run time) and says here-strings to interpreters are graded. (R6) a here-string to an interpreter that already runs a program (a script file, -c/-e) is data, as the heredoc arm treats it. (R7) a here-string operator glued to the interpreter's name is read. (R8) a unit case pins that a non-keyword `case` leaves a substitution readable. (R9) the CHANGELOG count is removed.
R1 (high) plugins/audit/hooks/guard-history-rewrite.py:406-431 (_stages), fed by _shell_pieces:256-260: _stages reads a `>` or `|` that came from inside a QUOTED word as a real operator. _shell_pieces splits every shlex token at _SEP_SPLIT, quoted ones included. Until now a split-out separator only ended an argument list, which is harmless. _stages gives it a new meaning: the rest of the quoted word becomes a redirect target. If that rest holds a `$`, _output_runs counts it as an unresolvable target, and every argument of the stage is re-read as a command line. Measured with the same fixture repo on main and on this branch: a commit message holding a forbidden git phrase next to `-> $VAR` or `output>$TMPDIR`, for example `git commit -m "guards: <git stash drop> -> $HOOK now denied"`, is allowed on main and DENIED here. This refuses a commit message, the shape the guard's own docstrings say must never be refused. Commit messages about this guard hold exactly these pieces. -> Build the stages from a quote-aware scan, so that only an UNQUOTED `>`, `>>`, `|` or `|&` is an operator. One way is to carry an 'unquoted' flag per piece out of _shell_pieces. Another is to derive stage boundaries with the quote tracking _quoted_substitutions already does. Add allow cases: a commit message holding a forbidden phrase plus `-> $X`, and one holding `>$TMPDIR`.
R2 (high) plugins/audit/hooks/guard-history-rewrite.py:451-469 (_output_runs), 572-584 (phrase pass in git_calls): The phrase pass assumes that every argument of a stage is what the stage PRINTS. That holds for echo and printf. It does not hold for grep, git log or sed, which print file content or history, not their argv. Joined with the unresolvable-target arm (`$` in the target), this refuses read-only commands. Measured, main allows and the branch DENIES: `git log --grep '<git stash>' > "$TMPDIR/hits.txt"`, `grep -n '<git stash drop>' SECURITY.md > "$TMPDIR/g.txt"` and `grep -rn '<git push --force>' docs > "$TMPDIR/g.txt"`. The same commands with a literal `/tmp/...` target are allowed. Writing a read's output to a `$TMPDIR` path is an ordinary shape, and a guard that refuses a READ gets routed around. -> Re-read as a command line only what the stage emits verbatim: the arguments of an echo or printf stage (past wrappers, via program_candidates), and a here-string or heredoc body fed to a cat-like printer. Leave every other program's arguments alone. Add allow cases for grep and git log redirected to a `$`-target. Keep gp36 and gp43 as the deny side.
R3 (med) plugins/audit/hooks/guard-history-rewrite.py:495, 500-513 (_open_case); consequence at decide():1132 and the text fallback: _open_case is not the shell's grammar. `case` is a keyword only in command position, but _CASE_WORD matches the bare word anywhere in the body. Checked by calling the function: git_calls on `echo "$(echo worst case)"; git log` returns None, so the whole command is unreadable. Two costs follow. (a) A VALID command is routed to the raw-text reading. Before this change, the substitution door to None was (almost) only an unclosed substitution, which the shell also rejects. (b) The raw-text reading is weaker than the parse for shapes that only the parse catches. decide() reads `calls or []`, so the verb that `xargs git` takes from stdin (STDIN_VERB) is never seen. A program name spliced from quoted pieces is also invisible to the `\bgit\b` patterns. So consider this shape: any double-quoted substitution holding the bare word `case` and no `esac`, placed in front of a spelling that only the parse refuses. It may now pass where main refused it. I did not run this, per your constraint; please verify. If it holds, SECURITY.md's line 'none of them lets through a command the 036e98e base refused' is at risk. -> Do this in _substitution_end rather than mark the body unreadable. Track `case` and `esac` only at command-word positions. While a case is open, a depth-0 `)` closes a pattern, so keep scanning to the `esac` and then to the real close. That reads the body the shell runs. Also consider refusing while a plan exists, rather than grading the raw text, when git_calls is None ONLY because of this rule. Add a regression case: a bare `case` argument in a substitution, followed by an xargs-stdin verb, stays denied.
R4 (med) plugins/audit/hooks/guard-history-rewrite.py:403, 406-431, 451-469: The stage model has structural gaps. All of them are described here by shape and none was run. (1) The clobber-override redirect (a greater-than immediately followed by a pipe) contains '|', so it is classed as a PIPE: its target becomes the next stage's program word and is never checked as a hook path. (2) A subshell or brace group whose closing token is a separate word from the pipe or redirect after it ends up as an EMPTY stage, so the phrase is unread. The glued spelling is caught, so the two spellings are graded differently. The same is true of a group on the receiving side of the pipe. (3) The receiving program is recognised only by the SHELLS tuple, which has five names. That misses the wider _config._SHELL_PROGRAMS (fish, mksh, ash), a shell named by a parameter expansion, and eval or source of a substitution that reads stdin. Yet _FILE_RUNNERS does include source and `.`. (4) A process-substitution target whose body is a shell is taken as a plain file name. (5) Hook-path matching is case-sensitive, but the filesystems of both the dev machine (macOS) and CI (Windows) are case-insensitive by default. program_name already folds case for exactly that reason. (6) `.husky/` is matched only as a leading prefix, not as a path segment, so a `./` or absolute spelling of a non-hook-named file under it is missed. (7) A glob character in the redirect target is not treated as unresolvable. -> Classify an operator by its whole spelling: a pipe is `|` or `|&`, and a run that starts with `>` is a redirect. Treat a group's closing token as passing its inner stage's words to the pipe or redirect that follows it. Use _config._SHELL_PROGRAMS, count an expansion in the receiver's program position as unresolvable (as the target arm already does), and add eval and source. Lower-case the hook basename and path before matching, and match `.husky` and `.git/hooks` as segments. Add glob metacharacters to the unresolvable test. Anything left unclosed goes into SECURITY.md (finding 5).
R5 (med) SECURITY.md:242-247: The desired outcome is that the list 'shrinks to what remains'. The new residual names only a file run by a later command and a hook directory holding a file not named as a hook. It leaves out residuals visible in this diff. A file can be written by a program that copies stdin to a named file argument (the tee shape) rather than by a redirect. The phrase can be split across several arguments that the printer joins. The finding-4 operator and group shapes are also missing. The document now reads as more closed than the code is. -> After findings 1-4 are settled, list every shape the phrase reading does not follow, one bullet per shape. Also state in the heredoc paragraph (around line 227, which still says only that a here-string is not read as a heredoc) that guard-secrets-read now grades a here-string fed to an interpreter as inline eval.
R6 (low) plugins/audit/hooks/guard-secrets-read.py:1085-1105 (_interpreter_herestrings): The grammar is wrong when the interpreter already has a program operand. When an interpreter runs a script file, `-c`/`-e` text or awk program text, the here-string is STDIN DATA, not the program. The heredoc arm this function says it mirrors exempts a plain script run through _config._plain_script_run. This arm does not, and _ANY_INTERPRETER includes awk and gawk, whose here-string is never their program. Measured: `python3 tools/redact.py <<< "<code-shaped text naming the env file>"` and `node scripts/lint.js <<< "..."` are allowed on main and BLOCKED on the branch, with the here-string refusal. The b5h5 allow case uses tr, so nothing pins this. -> Grade the here-string as the program only when the reader has no program operand. Reuse _plain_script_run for script runs, and treat a -c/-e option, or awk's first operand, as making the here-string data. Add allow cases for a script-file run and for awk.
R7 (low) plugins/audit/hooks/guard-secrets-read.py:1097-1100: _clause_words splits on blanks only. A here-string operator written with no blank between it and the interpreter's name makes a single word that does not start with `<<<`, so this arm never sees it. (Described by shape, not run.) The history guard's lexer splits `<` as a separator and is not affected. -> Find `<<<` inside a word, not only at a word's start: split the word at the operator and treat the left part as a reader word. Add a deny case beside b5h1.

It cannot go red if _open_case over-fires: an unreadable body goes to the raw-text reading, which also allows a body with no git in it. So it passes with the rule deleted or with the rule firing on everything. The other allow cases (gp37, gp39, gp40, gs14) were mutated over-fire; gs18 was not. -> Replace or supplement gs18 with a case where the parse and the raw-text reading disagree.
